title: First Sylow Theorem: Existence and Maximal Order
content: `sylow_existence` proves `Nonempty (Sylow p G)` — that a Sylow p-subgroup exists for every prime p. The proof is `Sylow.nonempty`, Mathlib's one-line instance. `sylow_card` gives the order formula: `Nat.card P = p ^ (Nat.card G).factorization p`, meaning the Sylow p-subgroup has order exactly $p^{v_p(|G|)}$ (the maximal power of $p$ dividing $|G|$). This is the sharpest possible: the Sylow subgroup is not just *any* p-power subgroup but the *maximal* one. The underlying Mathlib proof of existence proceeds by induction on $|G|$, using the class equation $|G| = |Z(G)| + \sum [G : C_G(g)]$ to reduce to smaller groups.
mathContext: If $|G| = p^k m$ with $p \nmid m$, then $\exists P \leq G$ with $|P| = p^k$. The order formula uses $(\text{Nat.card } G)\text{.factorization } p = v_p(|G|) = k$.

title: Second Sylow Theorem: Conjugacy and Isomorphism
content: `sylow_conjugacy` proves transitivity: for any two Sylow p-subgroups P, Q, there exists g ∈ G with `g • P = Q`. In Mathlib, G acts on `Sylow p G` by conjugation (the smul action), and `MulAction.exists_smul_eq` provides transitivity of this action — a one-line proof. `sylow_isomorphic` strengthens this to a group isomorphism: `Sylow.equiv P Q` produces a `MulEquiv` between the underlying subgroups. Together these show all Sylow p-subgroups are not merely conjugate but structurally identical (isomorphic as groups). The conjugacy proof in mathematics uses the action of P on G/Q by left multiplication and applies the fixed-point theorem for p-groups.
mathContext: $P, Q \in \text{Syl}_p(G) \Rightarrow \exists g \in G, Q = gPg^{-1}$. Equivalently: $G$ acts transitively on $\text{Syl}_p(G)$ by conjugation. The stabilizer of $P$ is the normalizer $N_G(P)$, so $n_p = [G : N_G(P)]$.

title: Third Sylow Theorem: n_p ≡ 1 (mod p) and Divisibility
content: `sylow_count_mod_p` proves `Nat.card (Sylow p G) ≡ 1 [MOD p]` using Mathlib's `card_sylow_modEq_one`. `sylow_count_dvd_index` proves $n_p \mid [G:P]$ via `card_sylow_dvd_index`. Together these give `n_p ≡ 1 (mod p)` and `n_p | |G|/p^k`. The congruence $n_p \equiv 1 \pmod{p}$ is the most subtle: the proof considers the action of any fixed Sylow p-subgroup P on the set Syl_p(G) by conjugation. Fixed points of this action are subgroups Q with P ≤ N_G(Q); by maximality, P and Q are both Sylow p-subgroups of N_G(Q), and by uniqueness in N_G(Q) (since P is normal in N_G(P)), Q = P. So P is the only fixed point, giving $n_p \equiv 1 \pmod{p}$.
mathContext: $n_p = |\text{Syl}_p(G)|$ satisfies $n_p \equiv 1 \pmod{p}$ and $n_p \mid [G:P] = m$. Together: $n_p \in \{1, p+1, 2p+1, \ldots\} \cap \{\text{divisors of } m\}$, strongly constraining group structure.

title: Normality, Uniqueness, and the Sylow Normality Equivalence
content: Three theorems establish the normality-uniqueness equivalence. `sylow_normal_of_eq` (the hard direction): if every conjugate of P is P itself (∀ g, g • P = P), then ↑P is normal. The proof uses `normalizer_eq_top` (normality iff normalizer is the whole group) and `Sylow.smul_eq_iff_mem_normalizer` to convert the conjugation action condition to normalizer membership. `sylow_normal_of_unique` applies when `Subsingleton (Sylow p G)` holds: all Sylow subgroups are equal by subsingleton, so `Subsingleton.elim` gives ∀ g, g • P = P. `sylow_unique_of_normal` is the converse: normal implies Unique, via `Sylow.unique_of_normal`. The practical consequence: if $n_p = 1$, P is normal (and vice versa).
mathContext: $n_p = 1 \iff P \trianglelefteq G$ (the unique Sylow subgroup is normal). Proof via `normalizer_eq_top`: $P \trianglelefteq G \iff N_G(P) = G$. The action condition $\forall g, gPg^{-1} = P$ is exactly $G \subseteq N_G(P)$.

title: Cauchy's Theorem and Cyclic Prime-Order Groups
content: `cauchy_from_sylow` proves Cauchy's theorem: if p is prime and p | |G|, then G has an element of order p. The proof uses Mathlib's `exists_prime_orderOf_dvd_card` — a one-liner. Historically, Cauchy proved this in 1845 using a direct combinatorial argument (the necklace/cycle counting proof). The Sylow-based proof: take a Sylow p-subgroup P (exists by Sylow I); P has order $p^k \geq p$; any non-identity element of P has order a power of p; raising to the right power gives order p. `group_of_prime_order_cyclic` then shows groups of prime order are cyclic, via `isCyclic_of_prime_card`: by Cauchy, there is an element of order p = |G|, generating the whole group.
mathContext: Cauchy (1845): $p \mid |G| \Rightarrow \exists g \in G, \text{ord}(g) = p$. For a group of prime order $p$: every non-identity element generates $G$ (since $\text{ord}(g) \mid p$ and $\text{ord}(g) \neq 1$, so $\text{ord}(g) = p$), so $G \cong \mathbb{Z}_p$.

title: Applications: Classifying Groups of Small Order
content: The summary section illustrates Sylow theory in action. For groups of order 15 = 3·5: $n_3 \mid 5$ and $n_3 \equiv 1 \pmod{3}$ force $n_3 = 1$; $n_5 \mid 3$ and $n_5 \equiv 1 \pmod{5}$ force $n_5 = 1$. Both Sylow subgroups are unique hence normal; their intersection is trivial (orders 3 and 5 are coprime), so $G \cong \mathbb{Z}_3 \times \mathbb{Z}_5 \cong \mathbb{Z}_{15}$. For order $p^2$: the counting forces the group to be abelian ($G \cong \mathbb{Z}_{p^2}$ or $\mathbb{Z}_p \times \mathbb{Z}_p$). For simple groups: if $n_p < |G|$ for some prime $p$ (so the Sylow subgroup is a proper normal subgroup), the group is not simple.
mathContext: Groups of order 15: $n_3 \in \{1\}$ and $n_5 \in \{1\}$ (by Sylow III), so $G \cong \mathbb{Z}_{15}$. Groups of order $pq$ with $p < q$ and $p \nmid q-1$: $n_q = 1$ (the Sylow $q$-subgroup is normal) and $n_p = 1$ (similarly), giving $G \cong \mathbb{Z}_{pq}$.
